result: ExoC3 treatment reduces caveolae density at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold (from 5.4 to 3.4 caveolae/µm²), with remaining caveolae evenly distributed and not accumulating around TEM tunnels.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31 and C62 are supported by quantitative electron microscopy data (Figure 1B-C) showing reduced caveolae density after ExoC3 treatment. The measurements include appropriate sample sizes (>175 µm² analyzed, n≥16 cells) and statistical analysis showing significant differences.

result: Depletion of caveolin-1 or cavin-1 increases TEM formation, with higher percentages of cells displaying TEMs (37.6% siCAV1, 36.4% siPTRF vs 28.8% siCTRL) and increased TEM density per cell (1.96 siCAV1, 1.36 siPTRF vs 0.91 siCTRL).
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C35-C37 are well-supported by quantitative imaging data (Figure 1E, Figure 1—supplement 2A) with large sample sizes (n=1400 cells, 8 experiments) and appropriate statistical analysis (mixed-effect logistic regression, p<0.0001). The inverse correlation between caveolae density and TEM formation is clearly demonstrated.

result: siRNA-mediated depletion shows differential effects: siCAV1 reduces both caveolin-1 and cavin-1 by ~80%, while siPTRF leaves ~50% of caveolin-1 unaffected. Neither treatment affects RhoA mono-ADP-ribosylation.
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1—supplement 1B-C) showing protein levels and RhoA modification status. The differential depletion is important for interpreting subsequent experiments, though the cross-depletion effect of siCAV1 on cavin-1 complicates interpretation of caveolin-1-specific effects.

result: ExoC3 treatment induces reorganization of actin cytoskeleton into a loose F-actin meshwork with increased mesh size (~0.2 µm²), with no significant differences between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C77 are supported by 2D STORM imaging data (Figure 2A-B) with appropriate quantification. The finding that caveolin-1 depletion does not exacerbate actin disruption is important for ruling out cytoskeletal mechanisms in the observed TEM phenotypes.

result: Caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition synergistically reduce cell height through increased spreading and decreased volume. ExoC3 treatment of siCTRL cells increases spreading by 36% and volume by 17%, resulting in 15% height decrease. siCAV1 and siPTRF treatments further enhance these effects, with siPTRF showing stronger effects on cell shape parameters in the absence of ExoC3.
evaluation: Claims C41-C46, C5, C63, and C80 are supported by quantitative measurements of cell area (Figure 3C), volume (Figure 3D), and calculated height (Table 1) with large sample sizes (n>152-698 cells) and appropriate statistical analysis. The mechanistic link between reduced cell height and increased TEM nucleation is logically sound and supported by the data.

result: Caveolin-1 specifically controls TEM opening speed and maximal width. TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1 cells compared to controls, with twofold higher opening speed (2.4 vs 1.1 µm²/s), while time to maximal diameter remains constant across conditions. siPTRF shows minimal effects on these parameters.
evaluation: Claims C6, C47-C50 are strongly supported by live-cell imaging data (Figure 4B-D) with appropriate temporal resolution (1 frame/second for opening speed measurements). The specific effect of caveolin-1 (but not cavin-1) on TEM dynamics is a key finding, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

result: Cav1-/- mice show increased susceptibility to S. aureus bloodstream infection with catalytically active EDIN-B. At LD50 (2.5×10⁷ CFU/m), Cav1-/- mice had lower survival with WT edinB (11/18 deaths) vs ΔedinB (4/17 deaths, p=0.0123), and catalytically active EDIN-B caused more deaths than inactive mutant.
evaluation: Claims C7, C52-C55, C64, and C95 are supported by mouse survival experiments (Figure 5) with appropriate group sizes and statistical analysis (Mantel-Cox test). The experiments with catalytically inactive EDIN-B mutant provide important controls establishing causality. However, the direct link to TEM formation in vivo remains inferential.

result: Caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30% (from 23.4±0.9 to 17.0±0.9 kBT) and increases membrane tension twofold, while cavin-1 depletion has no significant effect on bending rigidity. Theoretical modeling predicts 55% reduction in rigidity for siCAV1 and 15% for siPTRF.
evaluation: Claims C8, C56-C60, C65-C67, C78, and C91 are supported by membrane tether pulling experiments (Figure 6D) and theoretical modeling. The experimental measurements show clear differences with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for siCAV1 vs siCTRL. The discrepancy between experimental (30%) and theoretical (55%) predictions is acknowledged and attributed to model approximations (C68).

result: The difference between experimental (30%) and theoretical (55%) decreases in bending rigidity can be attributed to approximations in the theoretical model, including simplified treatment of membrane tension variation, cytoskeletal contributions, and TEM interactions.
evaluation: Claim C68 provides a reasonable explanation for the quantitative discrepancy between theory and experiment. The authors appropriately acknowledge model limitations, though this suggests the theoretical framework may need refinement.

result: Membrane tension and bending rigidity are the minimal mechanical parameters determining TEM nucleation and maximal size. Membrane tension drives TEM nucleation and initial opening speed, while bending rigidity sets maximal TEM aperture size. The minimal precursor tunnel size increases with bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension.
evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C22, C79, and C87 are supported by the combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements. The physical model (Equations 1-6) provides a framework consistent with the experimental observations, though some assumptions (e.g., limited cytoskeletal contribution) may be oversimplified.

result: The mechanisms by which caveolin-1 and cavin-1 regulate TEM nucleation differ: both reduce cell height favoring membrane apposition, but only caveolin-1 depletion increases membrane tension and decreases bending rigidity, further favoring TEM nucleation by decreasing the required minimal precursor tunnel radius.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 integrate multiple experimental findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The differential effects of caveolin-1 vs cavin-1 on membrane mechanics provide a clear explanation for their distinct impacts on TEM dynamics.

result: Caveolin-1 might contribute to plasma membrane enrichment with rigidifying lipids (cholesterol, sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids), and caveolae depletion with RhoA inactivation may release membrane-folding-driven mechanical constraints limiting cell spreading.
evaluation: Claims C75 and C85 are explicitly speculative ("might contribute," "may release"). While plausible based on known caveolae lipid composition (C73-C74), these mechanisms lack direct experimental support in this study. Further experiments are needed to test these hypotheses.

result: Discussion of potential mechanisms for caveolin-1's effect on membrane rigidity, including its membrane topology, reduced concentration in tunneling nanotubes, effects of protein inclusions on membrane rigidity, and enrichment of rigidifying lipids in caveolae.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74 and C76 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide context for interpreting the experimental findings, though they don't directly test mechanisms in this study.

result: Cell volume regulation during spreading: ExoC3-triggered spreading occurs with decreased cell volume, and caveolae depletion decreases cell volume independently of RhoA signaling. This is consistent with known mechanisms of cell volume homeostasis during spreading.
evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by cell volume measurements (Figure 3D) and appropriate citations. The finding that caveolae control volume independently of RhoA is novel, though the mechanism remains unclear.

result: Caveolin-1 expression has bidirectional effects on S. aureus susceptibility: OTULIN haploinsufficiency increases caveolin-1 levels, sensitizing cells to α-hemolysin, while caveolin-1 loss sensitizes to EDIN-B. Caveolin-1 expression is not regulated by RhoA signaling. EDIN-B is associated with hemoptysis in S. aureus pneumonia patients.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94, C96, and C99 are supported by appropriate citations (C92-C93, C96) and experimental data (C94: Figure 1—supplement 1A). The bidirectional effects highlight the complexity of caveolin-1's role in host-pathogen interactions, though the clinical relevance of TEMs remains to be established.

result: Background knowledge on endothelial barrier function, bacterial mART exotoxins, TEM formation mechanisms, caveolae structure and function, and effects of RhoA inhibition on vascular permeability.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C29, C97-C98 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings.

result: Summary statement: siRNA-mediated knockdown of caveolae components sensitizes endothelial cells to TEM formation triggered by RhoA inhibition.
evaluation: Claim C61 accurately summarizes the main experimental findings supported by multiple lines of evidence throughout the manuscript.

result: TEM nucleation requires apposition of basal and apical membranes, which is hindered by intermembrane distance (cell height).
evaluation: Claim C86 represents a fundamental physical principle underlying TEM formation, supported by the experimental observations linking cell height to TEM frequency.
